abstract: Multi-compartment protein targeting underlies the functional and metabolic flexibility of eukaryotic cells. However, how a single targeting region directs a protein to multiple cellular compartments remains poorly understood. A good example is membrane lipid biosynthesis: cardiolipin is normally synthesized in the mitochondrial inner membrane but has also been detected in the nuclear envelope of Tetrahymena. Here, we show that Tetrahymena cardiolipin synthase (TtCLS) localises to three distinct compartments. Systematic evolutionary and cell-biological analyses uncover a lineage-specific C-terminal targeting signal that expands the subcellular distribution of TtCLS across mitochondria, nuclear envelope and plasma membrane. We further show that its dynamic distribution among these compartments is regulated by phosphorylation. This multifunctional targeting architecture contains an amphipathic helix implicated in membrane association, which is structurally conserved across bacterial and eukaryotic CLS_PLD enzymes. Notably, this architecture remains compatible with conserved mitochondrial import systems across evolutionarily distant eukaryotes. Together, these findings uncover a previously unknown targeting architecture in which a single C-terminal region integrates overlapping and potentially regulatable localization determinants to target one protein across three different membrane systems.
